claims.statement: Kani bounded model checking (0.67.0, pure-kernel build without wasm plugins) shows that HttpPlugin::is_private_ip returns the same answer as an independent specification for every IPv4 address (all 2^32 values) and every IPv6 address (all 2^128 values), with the IPv4-mapped, NAT64 and 6to4 decode branches and the outright Teredo and NAT64 local-use blocks each exercised by a satisfiable kani::cover. The specification is a separate transcription of the IANA special-purpose registry snapshots committed under formal/vectors/, plus documented extra policy ranges and an explicit outright block of Teredo 2001::/32 and 64:ff9b:1::/48, and a normal test asserts its registry tables equal the maximal Globally Reachable False rows parsed from the committed CSV files (less the decoded IPv4-mapped row and rows inside a policy range).
claims.detector: set -e; cargo test --locked --no-default-features --lib -- plugins::http::ssrf_spec::tests; bash formal/run-kani.sh --harness plugins::http::ssrf_spec::kani_ssrf_proofs::ipv4_classifier_equals_spec_over_all_u32 --harness plugins::http::ssrf_spec::kani_ssrf_proofs::ipv6_classifier_equals_spec_over_all_u128
claims.does_not_establish: The drift lock covers the IPV4_BLOCKED and IPV6_BLOCKED tables and the classifier functions in http.rs (is_private_ip, is_ipv4_mapped_private, embedded_v4, ipv4_is_special_purpose, ipv6_is_special_purpose, v4_in_prefix, v6_in_prefix) plus the whole spec file; it does not cover doc comments above those items or the standard library conversions they call. That the IANA registry itself is correct or current: the CSV snapshots were fetched on 2026-10-08 and the spec tables are transcribed from them, so a later registry change is noticed only by the scheduled iana-snapshot-drift job (daily, not on pull requests), and the snapshots and tables are then refreshed by hand. That the spec is the right policy: it blocks multicast, 192.88.99.0/24, ::/96, fec0::/10 and the registry-reachable rows inside blocked rows (192.0.0.9/32 and 192.0.0.10/32 inside 192.0.0.0/24; 2001:1::1/128, 2001:1::2/128, 2001:1::3/128, 2001:3::/32, 2001:4:112::/48, 2001:20::/28 and 2001:30::/28 inside 2001::/23) on purpose, and it decodes NAT64 over 64:ff9b::/32 (not only the /96 well-known prefix) because the shipped decode does not check the middle 64 bits (kept as policy by a lead decision on 2026-10-09); both only over-block. The proof covers the pure classifier on an address value only. It does not cover DNS resolution or rebinding, redirects, proxies, hostname parsing, other URL spellings of an address (decimal, octal, bracketed forms handled by the URL parser), the HMAC plugin or any other caller, the separate internal_http allowlist (is_internal_destination_ip), or the config-time is_link_local_or_metadata_ip check. The detector runs each harness through formal/run-kani.sh, so it also fails when a harness reports no cover statement or an unsatisfiable one; that shows the harness is not vacuous, not that its covers are the right ones. Kani reasons about the Rust standard library address conversions as shipped in its toolchain; it does not cover the wasm-plugins build.

claims.statement: The tier order that the shipped engine scans (resolve_lazily: kill pre-check, then deny, prompt, allow, stopping at the first tier that matches) gives the same verdict as the pure precedence function over the full outcome set, for every sequence of up to 4 rule outcomes (kill, deny, prompt, allow, no-match; every multiset in every order), every sequence of up to 3 policy default actions and both engine defaults, and it asks no tier weaker than the one that decided and no tier at all under a kill flag. The pure function equals the written order kill > deny > prompt > allow > policy default > engine default and does not change when the lists are reordered; its fail-closed tail is never reached in that domain. Every verdict maps to its decision (kill, deny rule, deny default, engine default deny and the fail-closed tail all deny; prompt verdicts prompt; allow verdicts allow). The shipped evaluate equals the same order for every ordered list of up to two policies drawn from 48 shapes (kill flag, default action, any subset of always-deny, always-prompt and always-allow rules) under both engine defaults.
claims.does_not_establish: Only the precedence step. Whether a rule matches (URL, method, time window, rate limit, spend cap, action label) is outside it, and the domain is bounded at 4 outcomes and 3 policy defaults for the pure and lazy functions and at two policies of 48 shapes for the engine test. The engine test uses only always-matching rules and a fixed credential, so it does not cover rate-limit charging order beyond the lazy-scan check that no weaker tier is asked, and which matching rule's reason is reported within a tier follows storage order. The oracles are test code. The engine hands the lazy function at most one outcome per call by design; the multi-outcome equivalence is shown for membership of tiers, which is all the scan can observe. Layered Allow-RateLimit rules are conjunctive, which is the separate claim layered-rate-limits-conjunctive and not part of this one. The engine default applies only when no policy matches, and is not applied on top of a matching policy's default. The tail is shown to deny by the mapping test, not shown unreachable from the engine (it is unreachable only because any matching policy has a default action). The engine runs an unparseable-URL pre-check before the kill tier: a halted principal whose request URL cannot be canonicalised, under a policy with a URL deny or prompt rule, gets the unparseable reason instead of the halt reason. The outcome is still Deny and the pre-check is outside this claim.

claims.statement: For every list of up to 4 rule outcomes, every list of up to 3 policy default actions and both engine defaults, the precedence function returns the verdict with the highest rank in the order kill > deny > prompt > allow > policy default deny > prompt > allow > engine default, swapping two entries of either list does not change it, and it never returns the fail-closed tail; and the lazy tier scan the engine runs (resolve_lazily) returns the same verdict as the full function and asks no tier under a kill flag. All verdict kinds and the lazy cases are reachable in the harnesses (cover statements, enforced by the vacuity gate in run-kani.sh).
claims.does_not_establish: Bounded: lists longer than 4 outcomes or 3 defaults are not covered by the proof (the exhaustive test covers the same bounds). The rank table in the harness is written by hand. Nothing about rule matching, the verdict-to-decision mapping or the engine code that builds the default list and supplies the matcher. Swap-based order independence is checked for one swap of each list per run, not for every permutation at once. The detector runs each harness through formal/run-kani.sh, so it also fails when a harness reports no cover statement or an unsatisfiable one; that shows the harness is not vacuous, not that its covers are the right ones.

claims.statement: Policy::validate refuses a policy that contains a RateLimit condition at any depth (top level, inside and, or, not) unless its default action is deny, and accepts the deny-default shape. An exhausted Allow-RateLimit rule makes the engine's Allow tier stop matching; the request then falls through to the policy default in the engine (deny under deny, prompt under prompt, allow under allow), which is why the validation exists. A policy that fails Policy::validate when it enters the engine through add_policy, load_policies or load_policies_if_newer (for example a RateLimit policy stored with a non-deny default) is logged as a warning, once per policy and error, in the named unit test.
claims.does_not_establish: Validation refuses only at config load and on the admin API. The engine's own load paths (add_policy, load_policies, load_policies_if_newer) only log a failing policy, once per policy id, name and error in each process; the refusal of a stored RateLimit policy with a non-deny default happens one layer up, where the server loads from the vault, and is the claim stored-rate-limit-refused-on-load. The engine itself does not validate, so a policy added through PolicyEngine::add_policy without validation is not refused. Example tests over a few condition shapes. Layered rate limits are covered by layered-rate-limits-conjunctive. Default deny makes an over-limit request a denial because the whole Allow tier stops matching (every matching Allow rule's limits are enforced together, so another Allow rule in this or another matching policy cannot admit it; see layered-rate-limits-conjunctive). A Deny or Prompt rule that matches is an earlier tier and still decides first, and a rule whose only condition is a RateLimit allows every request on the credential until it is spent.

claims.statement: UrlMatch is evaluated on a canonical form of the request URL (url crate parse: scheme and host lowercased, IDNA, one trailing host dot dropped, default port dropped, dot segments resolved, fragment dropped, percent-encoding normalised so unreserved escapes are decoded and a stray % is encoded) with the caller's query map merged in sorted order, against a pattern canonicalised the same way. For generated equivalent spellings (host case, default port, trailing host dot, dot segments, encoded unreserved characters, fragment) the engine decision equals the decision for the plain spelling under Deny-prefix, Allow-prefix, Deny-glob and host-boundary-prefix rules. A prefix pattern that ends in * directly after a host matches that host on any port and path but not look-alike hosts (api.example.com.evil.net). A URL that cannot be canonicalised (including any URL with userinfo) never matches an Allow rule and is denied when a matching policy has a UrlMatch under a Deny or Prompt rule or under a Not. The http plugin sends the evaluated string and the hmac plugin sends the canonical base URL; both refuse a URL that cannot be canonicalised. For a UrlToken credential the http plugin sends the evaluated string with the secret in place of the literal {credential} placeholder and refuses the request when the URL with every literal {credential} replaced still canonicalises to a spelling of the placeholder in any letter case (percent-encoded, half-encoded, or with an escaped inner letter such as %7Bcr%65dential%7D), in the named unit tests. Risky patterns (star right after the host, star in the host, canonicalisation changing the meaning) log a load-time warning once per policy, pattern and rule kind; on a deny or prompt rule the line says the admin API refuses such a pattern when a policy is written and that this stored policy is still enforced as written, and on an allow rule it says the pattern is only warned; a scheme-less prefix that is a prefix of http:// or https:// (http*) is not reported as a star in the host, and any other scheme-less prefix (internal*) still is. An exact URL or path pattern with no wildcard and no query, and a pattern holding a { or } other than the literal {credential}, also warn (the exact-URL warning is not logged on an allow rule). The internal_http plugin composes and sends the evaluated string too (claim internal-http-sends-the-judged-string).
claims.detector: set -e; cargo test --locked --no-default-features --test url_canonical; cargo test --locked --no-default-features --lib -- policy::url_canon::tests policy::tests::url_warnings plugins::http::tests::test_prepare_request_sends_the_canonical_url plugins::http::tests::test_prepare_request_merges_query plugins::http::tests::test_prepare_request_url_token plugins::hmac::tests::test_hmac_sends_the_canonical_url
claims.does_not_establish: Property tests sample 512 generated spellings per run, they are not exhaustive and the oracle is the plain spelling under the same engine. It does not show the url crate parser agrees with what an upstream server does with the bytes (a server that treats %2F or path case differently is not modelled). How a glob is matched part by part (scheme, host, port, rest) is the url-glob-part-wise claim, with its own limits; a glob * in the path or query still matches / and ?. Warned patterns only log a warning at load; the refusal of warned patterns on Deny and Prompt rules (admin API, config file, stored load) is the claims policy-write-refuses-warned-deny-prompt-patterns and url-pattern-footguns-refused, and Allow rules are not refused (except under an odd number of not). A glob whose host holds ? is not canonicalised. The http, hmac and internal_http plugins send the canonical URL (internal_http: claim internal-http-sends-the-judged-string); the wasm plugin egress, ssh and postgres plugins do not use params url. The hmac plugin adds timestamp, recvWindow and signature after evaluation, and AWS SigV4 re-sorts query pairs for signing; those additions are not judged. For UrlToken requests the sent bytes equal the evaluated string apart from the secret on the tested URLs only, and the refusal of other placeholder spellings is shown on the listed spellings only. A secret holding /, ?, #, a backslash, %, whitespace or a control character is refused at store and at use (claim url-token-secret-structure-refused); other secrets are inserted as is and the substitution is checked for scheme and host only; a {credential} in a query-map value stays literal. The query map is merged only when it is a JSON object (a value that is not a string is judged as its JSON text; the http and hmac plugins refuse such a map). A prefix that ends in * inside a host (https://api.*, https://10.0.0*) is matched as the one host the parser reads from it, so a deny rule of that shape denies less than before (warned; refused on Deny and Prompt rules at admin-API write, config load and stored load, see url-pattern-footguns-refused). A pattern without a trailing * must match the query too, so a deny rule on an exact URL does not match the same URL with a query (such a Deny, and a Prompt in a policy whose default is not deny, is now refused). The meaning-change warning compares against a loose normal form and is shown on examples only; it can miss a change. The pattern is canonicalised at match time, not rewritten in storage, so list_policies still shows the operator's text. Evaluation of the URL stored in an approval at resume uses the same function but is not separately tested. The load-time warning is a log line and is not a refusal. The server call sites that build the judged URL (policy_url at request time and at approval resume) are not covered by the detector.

claims.statement: A UrlMatch glob (a pattern without a trailing *) is matched against a canonical URL that has an authority part by part: the pattern's scheme against the URL scheme, its host against the host, its port against the port (an authority is split at the last : outside [...], so an IPv6 literal host stays one host; a pattern without a port matches only a URL without one) and the rest against the path and query. A *, ? or [...] in the scheme or host therefore matches only inside that part, never /, ?, #, @ or the port. A pattern without a scheme is read with any scheme only when it starts with *; any other pattern without a scheme matches no URL with an authority. A URL without an authority (path-only) is matched as one string. The matcher is the same for Allow, Deny and Prompt rules. Shown in the named unit test on listed patterns (including *://api.example.com/x, which logs no warning, an IPv6 host and a ? in the host), in an engine test under an Allow, a Deny and a Prompt rule, and in a property test (512 cases per run) over generated other hosts, ports and carriers of the pattern host (path, query, %2F, @): a URL on another host is never matched under an Allow rule with default deny or a Deny rule with default allow, and the pattern's own host is.
claims.detector: set -e; cargo test --locked --no-default-features --test url_canonical star_in_host; cargo test --locked --no-default-features --lib -- policy::url_canon::tests::glob_wildcard_stays_in_its_component
claims.does_not_establish: Shown on the listed patterns and on 512 generated cases per run, not proved for every pattern or URL. Inside the host a wildcard still matches any run of host characters, dots included: https://*.example.com/x matches a.b.example.com and https://api.example.com*/x matches api.example.com.evil.net. Deny and Prompt globs match less than before: a glob without a port no longer matches a non-default port (https://*/admin misses https://h:8443/admin), and a glob without a scheme that does not start with * (ht*.example.com/x), which matched through the scheme before, now matches no URL with a host. A glob character class that spans a part boundary (a / or a : inside [...]) matches nothing, and the glob syntax reads an IPv6 literal written in a pattern host as a character class, not as that host. In a prefix pattern (trailing *) an earlier * is literal, so https://*.example.com/* matches no real host and a Deny or Prompt rule of that shape is dead (warned at load; the admin API, config load and stored load refuse it on a Deny or Prompt rule, see url-pattern-footguns-refused). A wildcard in the path or query still matches / and ?. The matcher assumes a canonical URL (no userinfo, no fragment); canonicalisation and what the plugins send are the url-match-canonical claim.

claims.statement: For three fixed known-answer cases, the vault master key derived by derive_key (Argon2id, version 0x13, 32-byte output, raw salt) decrypts an AES-GCM blob sealed under the key argon2 0.5.3 derived for the same password, salt and cost parameters: default cost, non-default cost with a non-ASCII password, and an empty password with an 8-byte salt. A whole vault file written by 0.5.3 with a persisted kdf header and one in the legacy shape with no kdf header both open and return the stored credential, and a newly created vault persists the same parameters (m=19456 KiB, t=2, p=1) that the 0.5.3 vault carries.
claims.detector: set -e; cargo test --locked --no-default-features --test argon2_kat -- --exact derived_keys_match_the_0_5_3_known_answers a_different_cost_parameter_does_not_open_the_blob vault_written_by_0_5_3_with_persisted_kdf_opens legacy_vault_without_kdf_header_opens new_vaults_persist_the_same_parameters_as_0_5_3; cargo test --locked --no-default-features --lib -- --exact crypto::encrypt::tests::default_kdf_params_match_argon2_crate_default crypto::encrypt::tests::key_roundtrips_through_persisted_params crypto::encrypt::tests::test_encrypt_decrypt_roundtrip crypto::encrypt::tests::test_wrong_key_fails crypto::encrypt::tests::test_encrypted_data_serialization
claims.does_not_establish: Only the fixed cases above, not every password, salt or cost setting, so a different argon2 release could still differ elsewhere. The fixtures were generated by this repository with 0.5.3, they are not the published Argon2 test vectors and not a check against another implementation. It covers the master-key KDF only: admin passwords use bcrypt and API keys use SHA-256, neither is touched. It does not show the AES-GCM layer, the vault file format or key rotation (rekey) are correct, and the Lean and Kani artifacts do not model the KDF. The KDF output length is pinned to 32 bytes explicitly, and the test would not notice a later change that stores a different length elsewhere. Salts shorter than 8 bytes are rejected by argon2 and are not exercised. Key equality is inferred from AES-GCM authentication succeeding under the derived key; the key bytes are not compared directly. Salts longer than 48 bytes behave differently: 0.5.3 rejected them (its PHC salt string holds at most 64 Base64 characters) and 0.6 accepts them; vultrino generates 16-byte salts, so no vault written by 0.5.3 carries one, and this case is not tested.

claims.statement: The admin policy write (POST and PUT /api/v1/policies, through build_policy) answers 400 invalid_policy, naming the rule and the pattern, and stores nothing, when a deny or prompt rule has a url_match pattern that canonical_pattern warns about, at the top level of the rule's condition or inside and, or or not. Shown on 9 warned patterns (a {a,b} glob among them; star in the host of a prefix and of a glob, a prefix ending right after and inside a host, dot segments, a star that cuts a percent escape, a host holding ?, a scheme-less prefix) x deny and prompt x 4 condition shapes x both routes. The same patterns on an allow rule are stored (201) unless the warned pattern sits under an odd number of not (not, not not not, inside and or or), where a dead pattern would allow every URL: that is refused 400 on both routes and stored nothing, while two nots store. Clean deny and prompt patterns in govder's compiled shape (and of action_match, url_match, method_match, including a relative path, https://*, a {credential} placeholder and *://host/x) are stored. An exact URL with no query is refused on a deny rule, and on a prompt rule in a policy whose default_action is not deny (a prompt on an exact URL in a default-deny policy, govder's compiled shape, is stored); that is shown in url-pattern-footguns-refused.
claims.does_not_establish: The refusal is as good as canonical_pattern's warnings: a pattern that matches less than it reads but draws no warning (a glob without a port that misses a non-default port) is accepted. Stored policies and config-file [[policies]] are refused by the claim url-pattern-footguns-refused, not by this detector; the engine's add_policy and load paths do not refuse. An allow rule is refused only under an odd number of not; any other warned allow pattern is stored and only warned. A deny or prompt rule whose url_match sits under not is refused too, although a dead pattern under not denies more, not less. Shown on the listed patterns and shapes, not every pattern. Which deployed vaults hold such a stored policy is not checked. An exact-URL Prompt in a default-deny policy is accepted; the engine matches Deny and Prompt patterns also without trailing query parameters (shown in url-query-never-weakens), so another Allow rule does not skip it.

claims.statement: A RateLimit policy (RateLimit at any depth) stored with an allow or prompt default is refused where the server loads stored policies: VultrinoServer::reload_policies returns PolicyError::Invalid naming the policy name, its id and the fix (vultrino policy deny-default <id>) and leaves the live set unchanged; the periodic refresh (refresh_policies_once) does not apply the set; load_stored_policies_at_startup returns the error, and `vultrino web` and `vultrino serve --mcp` (both start paths that load stored policies) exit non-zero with that message on stderr instead of starting. `vultrino policy deny-default <id>` sets the stored default to deny and keeps the rules, after which the policy loads; it reports no change on a second run and an error for an unknown id.
claims.detector: set -e; cargo test --locked --no-default-features --test web_smoke -- --exact stored_rate_limit_policy_with_non_deny_default_is_refused_on_load; cargo test --locked --no-default-features --test startup_security_integration -- --exact web_refuses_to_start_with_a_stored_rate_limit_policy_that_does_not_default_deny; cargo test --locked --no-default-features --test startup_security_integration -- --exact serve_mcp_refuses_to_start_with_a_stored_rate_limit_policy_that_does_not_default_deny
claims.does_not_establish: The RateLimit shape is the one this claim shows; a stored policy failing another validation rule (nested SpendCap, zero RateLimit dimension, degenerate TimeWindow) is still only warned and enforced as written. The refusal of a stored policy with a warned url_match pattern shares Policy::stored_load_refusal and is shown by url-pattern-footguns-refused. The engine's own add_policy and load paths do not refuse. The serve --mcp refusal is shown by one test with a stdin closed at start (a non-zero exit naming the policy), not by an MCP session. A running process that meets such a policy written by an older binary keeps its last good set and also stops picking up later valid changes in that vault until it is fixed. A reload after an admin write answers 500 reload_error while a refused policy is stored. Whether any deployed vault holds such a policy is not checked. The refusal does not change what a deny default means: an exhausted RateLimit still falls through to the other rules of every matching policy first.

claims.statement: vultrino's tenant assertion signer and verifier reproduce the shared golden vectors (vectors/tenant-assertion.v1.json, owned by govder and generated by an independent Python reference): the signer emits the reference payload and value, the verifier gives the reference verdict and reason on every accept and reject vector (jti exactly 16 lowercase hex, canonical decimal expiry, strict tenant segment), and the outbound client signs the path and query exactly as it puts them on the wire (a mock govder verifying the raw request-target accepts a base-path and re-encoded-query call).
claims.does_not_establish: Not key alignment between planes and not replay resistance (the verifier is pure). Examples chosen by the reference's author, not all inputs; govder's Go signer is checked against the same vectors in govder's own claim, not here.

claims.statement: vultrino's verifier on POST /api/v1/approvals/{id}/decision gives the reference verdict on the shared approval-assertion vectors (vectors/approval-assertion.v1.json, owned by feir-os, whose broker signs with the approval key M): the request-target as received, the exact body (approver, class, note), and the admin key's tenant are all bound, an assertion signed with the shared key F is refused, and a wrong tenant is refused.
claims.does_not_establish: Not that the approval route calls this verifier with M, the right tenant and the received request-target (a wiring property of the route, tested elsewhere), not the producer (feir-os's claim), and not who the approver really is.

claims.statement: vultrino's outbox signer sign_body reproduces the shared golden vectors (vectors/outbox-signature.v1.json, generated by an independent Python reference): sha256= followed by 64 lowercase hex digits of HMAC-SHA256 over the exact body bytes, and never a value the reference rejects. leria's meter-feed verifier and govder's approval webhook and activity-feed verifiers check copies of the same file in their own repositories; copy identity is checked only by the local --peer run.
claims.does_not_establish: Not key alignment, not that the signed body is the one delivered (delivery_body and the outbox store are separate), and not the consumers, which are claims in leria and govder.

claims.statement: A stored kill policy (or one stored after the work was admitted, even if lifted since) refuses a plugin dispatch, a streamed dispatch, an approval claim and an approval open, read from the vault under its cross-process lock immediately before the dispatch and independent of the process's in-memory policy engine: with two VultrinoServers over one vault standing in for two processes, an agent halted through one is not dispatched by the other (approval resume through the decision path, live call, streamed call), an approval claimed on the other process is refused and finalized, an approval opened before a kill does not run after the lift while a later one does, an approval cannot be opened for a halted agent, a kill that lands after a resume or live call has evaluated still blocks its dispatch, an engine that missed the kill in the same process is overruled, and a kill policy write through the admin route acknowledges the fence live with epoch >= 1 only when it reads back from the vault, on POST and on PUT (a replace raises the epoch; a policy that is not a kill carries no acknowledgement). The unkilled controls on the same fixture dispatch.
claims.detector: cargo test --locked --no-default-features --test kill_fence_integration && cargo test --locked --no-default-features --lib policy::kill_fence && cargo test --locked --no-default-features --test web_smoke -- --exact admin_policy_write_acknowledges_the_kill_fence_on_post_and_put
claims.does_not_establish: Rollout safety of the one-way vault format: the vault format (now 10, see vault-v9-migration) makes an older binary refuse the vault on open, but an older process already running keeps its loaded engine and is refused only where it takes the vault lock, so a vk_ API-key or LLM-proxy call on it can still dispatch after Contained; every process sharing the vault must be stopped (and the vault backed up) before the fence build starts. Kill marks are keyed by policy id (a re-stored id with a narrower pattern overwrites its mark). Dispatch lock contention is not measured (the fence read now takes the lock shared, see vault-fence-shared-lock-delta-read). Also: Several hosts (the vault is one file under one cross-process lock; a network storage backend answers the default fail-closed 'unsupported'), a dispatch whose fence vault read preceded the kill policy's vault write (the fence is the last check before the dispatch call, not a recall, so work already past that read runs), MCP, /execute and /llm entry points individually (they reach the shared execute_gated, execute_gated_streaming and resume_approved paths the tests drive; a new path that bypasses them is not covered), a halt that writes no kill policy, a kill epoch snapshot older than the durable value (conservatively refuses), or any CI run. Example-based tests over in-process servers and a counting plugin, not a proof; the model is govder formal/tla/KillFence.tla. Kill-mark garbage collection is a separate claim (vault-kill-mark-gc), with its own bounds.

claims.statement: VULTRINO_POLICY_REFRESH_SECS is accepted only as whole seconds from 1 to 86400 (surrounding whitespace allowed): 0, 86401, negative, fractional, suffixed, hex, empty and overflowing values fall back to the 5 second default, an accepted value sets the refresh interval, and the 'applied within the refresh window' message of a failed post-write reload quotes the effective interval, not the compiled default.
claims.does_not_establish: Only the parse and the effective-value accessors, on the listed inputs. It does not show the refresh loop ticks at that interval, that a running process re-reads the variable (it is read at startup), or that every message quotes it (only the reload_error message does).

claims.statement: POST /api/v1/approvals/{id}/decision answers every refused broker assertion (tampered body, another tenant, expired, past the verifier TTL ceiling, malformed header) with the same 401 invalid_tenant_assertion and the single message 'Invalid broker tenant assertion', records no sign-off, and writes the verifier's specific reason to the operator log.
claims.does_not_establish: Only the five listed failure shapes. Missing or duplicate assertion headers, an unconfigured approval secret (403 verified_approvals_disabled, a different and deliberately specific answer) and a wrong admin key are other branches and are not covered here. The log assertion relies on the test's tracing subscriber capturing the warning.

claims.statement: Replaying a captured signed approval decision (the exact request, same assertion, body and jti) while its assertion is still inside its TTL has no second effect: while the approval is open the replay does not fill a second recipe slot, and after the approval is decided it is answered 200 idempotent_replay and changes no status, sign-off or execution record. Vultrino therefore keeps no jti store for approval decisions: the dedup is the approval's own sign-off distinctness plus the decided-state idempotency check.
claims.does_not_establish: Only the shown shape: one two-teammate recipe, the same approver replayed. It does not cover a replay by a different party who captured the assertion and is bound to the same approver identity (the assertion binds the approver), a replay after the assertion's TTL (refused by expiry, tested in the verifier vectors), a replay of a deny against an approved request, or a decision made after the approval expired. The no-op argument depends on sign-off distinctness; a future change that lets one identity sign twice would reopen it.

claims.statement: The use PoP and params commitment length prefix (LP, uint32 big-endian) is exact or refused: every length that fits in 32 bits frames as itself and every longer length is refused with an error, never truncated to n mod 2^32 (so two different field sequences cannot share a preimage through a wrapped length).
claims.does_not_establish: The boundary is tested on the length function (0, 1, 255, 256, 65535, 65536, 2^32 - 2, 2^32 - 1 and several values at and above 2^32) and one framing example; no 4 GiB field is built, so the refusal inside lp is shown by construction of the same function, not by an oversized input. A bounded test, not a Kani proof or an exhaustive check over all lengths. The grant PoP v2 preimage has its own checked framing (lp_v2) and is not covered here.

claims.statement: vultrino's params_commitment (src/averin/pop.rs) reproduces every input-domain vector of vectors/params-commitment.v1.json, a byte-identical copy of averin's file pinned in vectors.lock, which is produced by an independent Python reference and also checked against averin's own commit::commit, and refuses every nonce string the file lists as rejected (wrong length, not hex, uppercase or mixed case hex, odd length, 0x prefix).
claims.does_not_establish: Only the listed inputs and only the input domain (vultrino never commits under another). Copy identity with averin's file is checked only by the local --peer run of check_vectors_lock.py, not by CI. It does not show the nonce is random or that the commitment hides a value.

claims.statement: vultrino's tenant-assertion verifier treats only a zero max TTL as 'use the default ceiling' and a positive sub-second max TTL as a ceiling of its whole seconds (0), the same as govder's Go verifier (pkg/tenantassert.Verify): with a 500 ms ceiling an assertion expiring this second verifies and one expiring a second or a minute later is refused ExcessiveTtl, never widened to the five minute default.
claims.does_not_establish: Only the ceiling arithmetic on a 500 ms value and three expiry offsets, in this repository's tests; govder pins the same behaviour in its own test, and the two are not compared by a shared vector (the shared vectors carry whole-second ceilings only). Not what ceiling the web route passes (govder.assertion_ttl capped by the broker maximum).

claims.statement: With a distinct approver-identity key configured (verified approver identities) and nothing written for enforce_separation_of_duty, separation of duty resolves to enforced, and the decision route refuses a self-approval (approver equal to the requester's identity) with 409 approval_not_decidable and writes nothing, with no explicit flag, while an explicit false records it; an explicit false in [approvals] keeps it off and the startup line says so; without verified identities (dev mode) the default stays off and the startup line says so; an explicit true holds in every case. Separation of duty compares the approver only with the requesting agent's own identities (principal name, agent label, principal ids): the agent's directory owner is NOT a self-approval, so an owner approves their own agent's request under the enforced default, and the requesting agent itself is still refused. A stamped recipe with exclude_owner true refuses the directory owner (409, nothing recorded) even with the flag off, a deny by the owner is never blocked, and exclude_owner defaults to false.
claims.does_not_establish: That main.rs calls apply_sod_default with the live key posture before serving (a wiring line, covered by the four-plane e2e self-approval leg, not by this detector or a drift lock); that the approver identity is authenticated (the broker signs only under a real IdP; the dev escape VULTRINO_ALLOW_SHARED_APPROVAL_KEY and FEIR_OS_ALLOW_DEV_VERIFIED_APPROVERS are documented dev/test postures that weaken it); that requester and approver are compared on the same identity namespace (an agent identity that differs from the approver's IdP subject is not a self-approval); and nothing about [approvals] enabled. The same-aggregator-key refusal (one key filling two seats of a two-person rule) is independent of this flag and is not established by it. The CLI approve/deny path never enforces separation of duty regardless of this setting (decide_approval in src/main.rs passes false).

claims.statement: An admin write to the vault appends one encrypted log record that holds only the records the write changed, and fsyncs that record, so the bytes written, the records written and the decrypt work of one write do not grow with the number of unrelated stored use tokens, policies or kill marks. With the compaction threshold held out of the way: storing one policy writes exactly one record and one log line, decrypts nothing and leaves the snapshot byte-identical at 0, 60 and 400 stored tokens, with equal bytes written (within 16 bytes); a 40-write provision burst writes 40 records, decrypts nothing and costs the same at 0 and 300 stored tokens; a mutation that changes nothing writes nothing; a mutation that returns an error rolls its changes back in memory (an inserted record gone, a removed record restored) and commits nothing, and a reopen sees the pre-mutation state. In debug builds every mutation in the whole unit-test suite also replays the vault files from scratch and requires the result to equal the in-memory state. The vault_cost example reports the same counters against vault size.
claims.does_not_establish: Wall-clock latency or throughput: every assertion counts bytes, records, decrypts and files, never time, and the benchmark prints counters, not durations. The CPU cost of a write: the in-memory shape validation and the kill-fence diff still walk the in-memory records, so the CPU per write is not constant (it is no longer an encrypt-and-fsync of the whole vault). Amortised compaction: when the log passes max(256 KiB, snapshot size) one write rewrites the whole snapshot, so the worst single write is still O(vault) and only the average is O(record); the example's build_B/write column shows the average. The separate outbox file, which is still rewritten whole by its own store. Filesystem fsync honesty or power-loss durability. Any CI run.

claims.statement: A vultrino process that dies at any step of a vault log append or compaction leaves a vault that reopens with every acknowledged write present and no torn record. For a kill-policy write (three changes: the policy, the kill epoch, the mark) killed before the append, after half a line, after a full unsynced line and after the fsync with the acknowledgement lost, the reopened vault has all three changes or none, still holds the earlier credential, tokens and epoch, and accepts and persists a further write. A torn (unterminated) tail is ignored by a reader without modifying the file, is truncated by the next writer, and never appears as a record. A crash at each of the four compaction steps, and between the snapshot rename and the log reset (where the log still holds records the snapshot already folded in), reopens with nothing lost and continues the sequence. A missing, reordered or bit-flipped terminated record fails the open closed. Rekey folds the log, never decrypts old-key records, and a crash between its rename and the log reset still opens under the new password. A crash during the v9 migration at three steps reopens with every record. A write whose append or fsync fails in a live process takes its line back out of the log (best effort), so the next reader does not treat it as committed. A process that loses the race to create a fresh vault opens the winner's vault instead of overwriting it. A panic inside a mutation (for example in the middle of a kill lift) rolls the in-memory state back before it unwinds, so readers keep the kill and a later unrelated write does not commit the abandoned change. A wrong master password with the averin stores enabled and a non-empty queue is reported as a decrypt error, because the snapshot is decrypted before the queue is replayed.
claims.does_not_establish: Power-loss durability of any real filesystem or disk: a crash is an injected error at a named step that leaves the files exactly as written (the page cache is not dropped, fsync is assumed honest). Crashes at steps the injection points do not name, or inside the standard library. Detection of a vault rolled back by replacing the snapshot and log with older copies, or of a log truncated at a record boundary: both are accepted by the format, as a replaced vault file always was. A terminated final line damaged by a crash or bit rot fails the open closed instead of being recovered; an operator must truncate it after checking. Behaviour under concurrent writers in several real processes beyond what the advisory lock already serialises. Any CI run. The take-back of a failed append is best effort: if the truncate itself fails after an fsync error, the line may remain and be read as committed by the next reader. A panic raised inside the commit itself (as opposed to the mutation closure) is rolled back by the same path but has no dedicated test. An invalid record in a delta replay drops the process's whole in-memory view (readers see nothing and deny) and forces a full reload; this is not covered by a test.

claims.statement: The dispatch kill-fence read takes the cross-process vault lock shared, not exclusive, and reads only what changed since this process last looked. An unchanged vault costs the fence zero decrypts, zero bytes written and zero fsyncs; after another handle appends one record the fence decrypts exactly that one record and sees the kill it carries; another handle's kill and its lift are seen without a reload (the lifted kill still refuses work admitted before it); a compaction by another handle is picked up. A fence read completes while another handle holds the lock shared, and waits while another handle holds it exclusive, so committed state is still what the fence sees. A v9 process rewriting the snapshot under a running v10 process is refused (fail closed), including right after a compaction when the log is empty and its length equals the process offset, so the snapshot version is the only sign. A kill write that is waiting for the vault lock holds the writer-intent gate (a sidecar lock file taken exclusively before the vault lock, released once the vault lock is held), and every fence read passes through that gate before its shared lock, so a fence read that starts after a waiting kill write queues behind it and the write commits first; with eight handles looping fence reads, a kill write on another handle completes within five seconds.
claims.does_not_establish: The TLA+ model govder formal/tla/KillFence.tla was not re-run: its assumption (a fence read observes every kill write committed before it) is argued to be preserved because writers still commit under the exclusive lock and a shared read excludes them, not re-checked mechanically. Handles in one process stand in for processes: the lock is a flock on separate file descriptors, which conflicts between descriptors in one process exactly as between processes, but no test starts a second OS process. Lock behaviour on network filesystems, FUSE or Windows. The in-memory kill epoch read at admission, which is not synced from disk (it can only be stale-low, which refuses more). Dispatch throughput or contention, which is not measured. Any CI run. Detection of another process's commit relies on the snapshot's (mtime, length, inode) token plus the log length, so a filesystem with coarse timestamps that rewrites a snapshot to the same length within one tick is not supported (before the log this affected only the read cache; it now covers writes and the fence). Writer starvation is not bounded by proof: flock gives no writer preference on the gate either, so taking the gate is fast in practice (readers hold it for a few syscalls; a probe with 32 looping readers saw 5 kill writes wait 11 to 29 ms), not guaranteed. The test uses handles in one process (eight looping readers, five seconds), not several OS processes, and it relies on flock on a local filesystem. A locked read nested inside another locked read on one thread can deadlock against a waiting writer; only a debug assertion guards it. Writers queue one at a time on the gate. In-process lock-free readers (get, get_by_alias, get_policy, kill_fence_epoch) block for the duration of a write, including one log fsync, and for a whole-snapshot encrypt and fsync when the write triggers compaction; a fence catch-up after a foreign write runs shape validation and index rebuild over the whole vault under the in-process cache lock.

claims.statement: A vault write-ahead log that is removed, or shortened below what a running process has already applied, while the snapshot is unchanged, never turns a halted agent clear: the next dispatch fence read and every write fail closed (Unavailable), and keep failing on repeat, in both cases (log deleted; log truncated to 0 bytes and to 1 byte, with a stored kill in the log). A v10 snapshot whose log file is missing is refused at open, naming the log, and the refusal creates nothing. Vault creation, migration and compaction create the (empty) log before the snapshot is renamed in, so a crash right after the rename leaves a log the next open finds and an empty file, not a missing one.
claims.does_not_establish: Log loss while no vultrino process is running: a log truncated at a record boundary (or by a torn tail) still opens as the shorter state, because the snapshot does not record the log's length; only a missing log is detected at open. An attacker who can write the vault directory and puts back an older vault file together with its older log. A log replaced by a different file of at least the same length while the snapshot is unchanged and the length equals the applied offset. Filesystems that report a stale length. A crash between the log creation and the snapshot rename leaves an empty log beside the old snapshot, which is accepted (it holds nothing). Any CI run other than the recorded one.

claims.statement: A vultrino process that has loaded the vault (it holds a snapshot token) and then finds the vault file itself gone never turns a halted agent clear: the next dispatch fence read and every write fail closed (Unavailable) and keep failing on repeat while the file stays gone, both when the log still holds the kill and right after a compaction when the log is empty too, and a write does not recreate the vault file. The decision is made on the same stat as the load, so a deletion landing between two looks, or right after a compaction's rename, is refused too and the token stays set. The refusal ends when a vault file reappears: the refusing process then reloads and accepts any file that decrypts under its key.
claims.does_not_establish: Deletion while no vultrino process is running: a process started after the deletion finds no vault and starts one fresh, as for any vault that never existed. Offline truncation of the .wal tail at a record boundary without a durable anchor: accepted limitation, because filesystem write access is outside the threat model (stated in LIMITATIONS). Replacing the vault file with an older copy, or a file replaced by a different one between two looks (the snapshot token then changes and the process reloads as for a compaction). A vault file recreated by a new process with a new salt: the refusing process then keeps failing with a decryption error (not Unavailable) while the new process answers Clear. Another process's view: only the process that loaded the vault refuses. Any CI run other than the recorded one.

claims.statement: If a vault write panics after its log record is durable and the offsets have advanced, the rollback alone would restore the pre-write kill state while the process believes it is current with the log; the process instead marks its view unloaded, so the next fence read reloads from the files and answers Halted for the durable kill, and later reads, writes and a reopen agree with it. A panic inside a mutation closure rolls back and also reloads. A commit error reloads too, conservatively, with no observable difference from the offsets alone (the failed append never advances them), so that reload is pinned by a flag check and is not a semantic claim.
claims.does_not_establish: Failure points other than a panic injected right after the log append and one in the closure; no production commit error occurs after the offsets advance, so the commit-error reload has no killing mutant. A panic or error inside the append itself is not injected. The reload is conservative: any commit error, including one before the record was written, reloads. A process killed at the same points is covered by vault-log-crash-consistency, not here. Any CI run other than the recorded one.

claims.statement: Kill marks are garbage-collected only when provably dead, and a collected mark never re-admits killed work. A mark is collected only when its kill policy is no longer stored as a kill, its timestamp is at least 24 hours old (an unstamped mark is never collected, and the boundary is inclusive), and no approval that can still be claimed (open, approved and not executed, or executing) was admitted at an epoch below the mark's epoch (an approval with no recorded epoch counts as epoch 0). A stored kill policy's mark is kept however old, including when a lifted id is killed again. The kill epoch is never lowered, the drop is durable across a reopen, work admitted at the current epoch stays clear, a later kill still halts, and an approval opened before a lifted kill is refused until it finishes, after which its mark is collected. The approved-but-not-executed and executing cases are pinned by their own tests: such an approval keeps the mark through GC and a reopen, and its claim is still refused.
claims.does_not_establish: The govder TLA+ model formal/tla/KillFence.tla: it models the fence as an epoch comparison that is never collected (there are no marks and no collection in it), so its NoStaleDispatch property does not cover a collected mark; in code the guarantee for a live in-flight call rests on the 24 hour grace. That grace compares the storing process's wall clock (stored_at) with the collecting process's wall clock, so a clock that steps forward, or a host that was behind when the kill was stored, shortens the effective grace. That every holder of an admission epoch is counted. Approvals are counted explicitly; a live call in flight inside one process holds its epoch only in memory, and is covered by the 24 hour grace alone, so a request that stalled for more than 24 hours between admission and dispatch could be re-admitted after a collected kill. Marks written by a build that does not stamp them. How often garbage collection runs (the periodic vault GC tick, not tested here). Mark keying by policy id, unchanged: a re-stored id with a narrower pattern still overwrites its mark. Any CI run.

claims.statement: A real v9 vault file (generated by the v9 build, tests/fixtures/vault-v9) opens in this build with every credential, use token, stored policy, the kill epoch and a lifted kill's mark intact, and the lifted mark still refuses pre-kill work. The first open copies the v9 file byte-for-byte to <vault>.v9.bak (atomically, owner-only) and rewrites the vault as v10 (a snapshot plus an empty log); a later open neither migrates again nor overwrites the backup; writes after the migration persist. Marks written before v10 carry no timestamp and are stamped at migration so they age out 24 hours later. A v10 vault is refused by a v9 build's version gate (its supported maximum is 9), and a vault whose snapshot is rewritten by an older build under a running v10 process is refused. A log file left beside a pre-v10 snapshot (as after a rollback that kept the log) is never replayed: the open fails closed naming the real files, and nothing on disk changes. A backup that already exists is never overwritten: if it differs from the current file the copy goes to a unique name.
claims.does_not_establish: Rollback after new writes: restoring the backup with the v9 build loses every write made since the migration (the format is one-way by design). The real file names are <vault>.wal and <vault>.v9.bak with the extension of the vault file replaced (credentials.enc gives credentials.wal and credentials.v9.bak). A rollback that restores the vault file but leaves the log is refused at open, not repaired; the operator deletes the log. A fixture that exercises approvals, workload grants or idempotency records (the fixture holds credentials, tokens, policies and kill marks; the older-version migrations are covered by the existing v6 tests). That the v9 binary really refuses the file: the test asserts the version number the v9 gate compares against, it does not run a v9 binary. A mixed-build fleet running during the migration, which must be stopped first. Any CI run.

claims.statement: GET /api/v1/posture answers only to a global (untenanted) admin key and reports, from the running process, the policy engine's live default (deny or allow), whether separation of duty is enforced, whether the approver-identity key is configured, distinct from the govder key, or on the shared-key escape, which tenants are in observe mode, which enforced policies have a RateLimit condition with a non-deny default, whether an explicit upstream proxy is configured (never its URL) and that the plugin egress client does not honour the ambient proxy variables (the field plugin_ambient_proxy_honoured; the approval notifier client also ignores them, the outbox, govder and averin clients still do), whether an inbound [identity] header is configured and its signing key is present, the [averin] D8 evidence floor mode as configured and as in effect (it takes effect only with d8_complete_evidence on), the vault format version this binary writes, and the rustc and git commit it was built with. The report holds booleans, counts, identifiers and secret fingerprints only (see secret-fingerprint-report).
claims.detector: cargo test --locked --no-default-features --test web_smoke -- --exact posture_requires_an_operator_key_and_reports_the_live_engine posture_refuses_a_tenant_scoped_key posture_lists_a_stored_fail_open_rate_limit_policy posture_reports_a_non_deny_engine_default_as_it_is && cargo test --locked --no-default-features --lib -- web::posture::tests
claims.does_not_establish: That the process enforces what it reports beyond the code paths those fields are read from: the report reads the engine and config objects the request handlers use, it does not re-run a policy decision. It does not prove the approver key is strong, rotated or known only to the broker, that the vault file on disk is at the reported format version (the field is the version this binary writes, a vault is migrated when opened), that no second vultrino process shares the vault (a process cannot see its peers), or that a deployment actually calls the endpoint: that is the feir-os posture verifier. The git commit is the one the build script saw; a build from an archive reports unknown. The detector runs the endpoint against an in-memory test router, not a deployed binary. The egress and identity fields report configuration, not what any request did.

claims.statement: In the engine's Allow tier every matching Allow rule's top-level RateLimit (a bare rule, or inside and at any and depth) joins one guard set per request, de-duplicated by (max, window_secs). The request is admitted only if every guard in the set has room, and then all are charged under one lock; a refused request charges none. Tested on the real engine: a 2 per minute and a 100 per day rule deny the third call whichever rule is stored first; the same with the tight cap on the long window; two matching policies with one limit each; a refused request leaves the long counter at the admitted count; identical dimensions are charged once; a rule whose action does not match is not charged; an unlimited Allow rule that also matches, in the same policy or in another matching policy, does not switch a matching limit off; the post-approval resume checks and charges nothing; a zero-sized limit in the set refuses without charging its valid sibling.
claims.does_not_establish: Example tests over the listed rule shapes, not an exhaustive check, and the Kani precedence harnesses do not model the Allow tier's guard set. A RateLimit written inside or or not is not part of the guard set and keeps its inline evaluation. Counters are per process and in memory, so two vultrino processes enforce their own caps (the cross-process shared limit is a separate item). The fixed-window transition is covered by the rate-limiter trace vectors, not here. Which matching rule's reason is reported when several match follows storage order. The tests run the engine directly; that the server calls it on every admission path is covered by the permit-kernel claims. The Allow tier evaluates every Allow rule's non-guard conditions, so a RateLimit written inside or or not is charged on every request even when another rule matched or when the guard set then refuses it: that over-charges (the fail-closed direction) and is not tested for exactness.

claims.statement: A failed outbox append is counted and later announced. In the unit tests of the real file storage, with every outbox write forced to fail by a directory sitting on the writer's temp path: each failed append returns an error and increments the lost counter and the pending-gap counter; no marker can be written while writes fail; after the writer recovers the next successful append is followed by exactly one meter.lost event carrying lost_count, the first and last failure times and the distinct lost event types, with the sequence still gap-free; the pending gap returns to zero while the lifetime counter stays; no second marker appears for the same loss; a second outage gets its own marker. GET /api/v1/health reports meter_lost_total and meter_gap_pending (and stays status ok), GET /api/v1/ready reports meter_gap_pending, and the posture report carries the same counters under meter. GET /api/v1/events carries meter_gap_pending on its envelope: 0 when healthy, the pending count while appends fail (with no events and no marker yet), and 0 again once the marker has been written. End to end, with the outbox writes failing while a real metered LLM call runs through the proxy: the call is still admitted (200), both of its meter events (api-calls and the priced token event) are counted as lost, GET /api/v1/events and GET /api/v1/health report meter_gap_pending 2 while no event exists, and after the writer recovers the next call's first append is followed by one meter.lost marker with lost_count 2 and event_types [meter.observed], after which meter_gap_pending is 0.
claims.detector: cargo test --locked --no-default-features --lib -- --exact storage::file::vault_tests::a_failed_append_is_counted_then_announced_by_a_meter_lost_marker storage::file::vault_tests::a_second_outage_gets_its_own_marker web::posture::tests::report_carries_the_meter_append_loss_counters && cargo test --locked --no-default-features --test web_smoke -- --exact test_health_and_ready_report_a_failed_outbox_append test_event_feed_reports_pending_meter_gap_while_appends_fail && cargo test --locked --no-default-features --test llm_proxy_integration -- --exact v2_a_metered_call_during_an_outbox_outage_is_counted_announced_and_marked
claims.does_not_establish: The counters and the pending marker are held in memory: if the process exits before an append succeeds again the marker is never written, and a consumer's stale watermark is the only remaining signal. Failures are produced by one injected fault (an unwritable temp path), not by a real full disk or a failing fsync. Only the direct append path is counted; events staged in the vault and drained later are retried by the reconciler instead. That a consumer acts on the marker is the leria claim for its poller, not this one. Says nothing about events lost while the process is down or about the outbox being tampered with. Failed appends do not fail the metered call: vultrino keeps admitting calls during an outage, and the pending count is the only in-band signal until the marker (so the fail-open choice stands and the consumer's watermark is the control). The count is in the unsigned envelope. That the consumer acts on it is the leria claim meter-lost-marker-holds-as-of.

claims.statement: A streamed LLM call is charged tokens even when the provider's usage trailer does not reach the client. With a gated test upstream: when the client hangs up before the trailer, the producer keeps draining the upstream and the token event carries the provider's exact counts (OpenAI-style trailer 11 and 22; Anthropic message_delta output 77 rather than message_start's provisional 1) with no estimated marker; when the stream ends without any trailer the token event carries an estimate (3000 generated bytes give 1000 output tokens, input from the request size) and dims.estimated is true; when the drain's idle cap fires first the call is charged an estimate and the drain stops at the cap; a halted stream and a stream with no trailer on the buffered fallback are charged estimates. In unit tests: an Anthropic message_start usage is not final, an OpenAI trailer, a Responses response.completed and an Anthropic message_delta are, a null usage is not; the estimate counts generated delta text and not framing, prefers the provider's real counts, is capped by the request's own output limit and is never zero; the estimated payload carries dims.estimated and the exact one does not. A halt that lands after the client has already hung up, while the producer is draining, closes the upstream within one chunk (the upstream is dropped, not drained to its idle cap) and the call is charged an estimate.
claims.detector: cargo test --locked --no-default-features --lib -- --exact outbox::tests::anthropic_message_start_usage_is_provisional_until_the_final_delta outbox::tests::openai_trailer_and_responses_completed_are_complete_but_a_null_usage_is_not outbox::tests::estimate_counts_generated_text_not_framing_and_prefers_real_counts outbox::tests::estimate_falls_back_to_raw_bytes_when_a_giant_line_stopped_parsing outbox::tests::request_output_limit_is_read_from_every_provider_shape outbox::tests::estimated_token_payload_carries_the_marker_and_the_normal_one_does_not && cargo test --locked --no-default-features --test llm_proxy_integration -- --exact vul01_disconnect_before_the_trailer_still_charges_the_providers_exact_count vul01_a_provisional_anthropic_output_count_is_not_charged_as_final vul01_a_stream_that_ends_without_any_trailer_is_charged_an_estimate vul01_the_drain_is_bounded_by_the_idle_cap_and_then_estimates llm_streamed_without_a_usage_trailer_is_charged_an_estimate llm_streamed_halt_cancels_midstream vul01_a_halt_after_the_hangup_closes_the_draining_upstream_at_once
claims.does_not_establish: The estimate is a rough one (about one token per three generated bytes, rounded up on purpose), not the provider's count: it over-charges typical text and can still under-charge text that tokenises very densely. It needs a model from the request or the stream to be priced; a stream with neither meters the api-calls event only. The upstream is a test double with the OpenAI and Anthropic shapes, not a live provider; Gemini and the Responses API shapes are covered by the accumulator unit tests only. The drain is bounded by the same idle, total and byte caps as a live stream, not by a new cap, and a hostile client can hold an upstream stream open for that long. A halt closes the upstream (stopping generation) and is charged an estimate rather than drained, both while forwarding and while draining after a hang-up. The estimate counts text under delta keys only, so a provider that streams text elsewhere (Gemini candidates parts) estimates low, hidden reasoning tokens are not counted, and a provider that reports cumulative usage on every chunk would be read as complete on the first one; today only stream:true requests take this path and the OpenAI and Anthropic shapes are the tested ones. Says nothing about leria pricing or deduplicating the event, which is leria's claim.

claims.statement: Every secret-bearing outbound HTTP client in the product source ignores the ambient HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and ALL_PROXY variables: the guarded client built by build_guarded_client (with all three pointing at a recording server, a request to a reachable target goes directly and the proxy sees none), and the averin, govder, outbox, internal_http, approval-notifier, Telegram callback poll and request-CLI clients, each of which calls no_proxy (a scan of the non-test source fails on any client builder without it). The only proxy is the explicit VULTRINO_UPSTREAM_PROXY opt-in (an http:// or https:// URL whose host is an IP literal, a host name stopping client construction; any other value stops client construction instead of falling back to a direct connection). With it set, an https:// target is routed through it and an http:// target is never handed to it. VULTRINO_UPSTREAM_PROXY_CA_FILE adds a private CA for the proxy's certificates and stops client construction when it is set without the proxy, unreadable or not PEM. HttpPlugin::validate_url_ssrf refuses a plain http:// target in every mode (no proxy, a remote proxy, a loopback proxy), after its host checks, so an injected credential never crosses a public network in clear text. GET /api/v1/posture reports whether the opt-in is set, never its URL. While it is set, HttpPlugin::validate_url_ssrf and HmacPlugin::validate_url_ssrf refuse a target host whose local lookup fails or returns no address (proxy_needs_resolution); with no proxy set the same host is admitted and fails at connect time. The other secret-bearing clients take an operator-configured URL and refuse a plain http:// endpoint that is not a loopback or private address, in every mode: AverinClient::new and GovderClient::new at construction, the outbox url and the approval webhook url at config load, and the request CLI for VULTRINO_API_URL (plain_http::check: https is admitted, http only for a loopback or private IP literal or a name that does not resolve to a public address); for an http:// URL the client also gets a connect-time resolver that returns only loopback or private addresses, so a name that later resolves to a public address fails the connection. A scan fails on any product client builder that does not go through plain_http::guard. GET /api/v1/posture also reports egress.upstream_proxy_ca_configured.
claims.detector: set -e; cargo test --locked --no-default-features --test upstream_proxy; cargo test --locked --no-default-features --test no_ambient_proxy_clients; cargo test --locked --no-default-features --lib -- plugins::http::tests::upstream_proxy_value_is_parsed_strictly; cargo test --locked --no-default-features --lib -- plain_http::tests
claims.does_not_establish: That a proxy chosen with VULTRINO_UPSTREAM_PROXY behaves: it resolves the target host itself, so the connect-time resolver guard does not cover that hop (the admission-time URL check still runs) and the operator trusts the proxy, and a CA named with VULTRINO_UPSTREAM_PROXY_CA_FILE is trusted for every https target of the guarded client while the proxy is set. The https route through a real CONNECT tunnel is not exercised by this detector, only that the client hands https targets to the proxy and that the CA settings fail closed; the four-plane credential-canary e2e drives real tunnels with a test CA. The plain http:// refusal for agent-chosen URLs is on HttpPlugin::validate_url_ssrf (the http plugin, which the LLM proxy and capabilities use); for the operator-configured endpoints it is plain_http::check at build or config load plus the connect-time private-only resolver. A private or loopback http:// endpoint is still allowed and carries its secret in clear text on that network (a compose network or loopback), and a name that resolves to a private address and an https certificate are not otherwise validated. The scan of client builders is textual, like the no_proxy scan, and the request CLI is checked by a source assertion, not by running it. The no_proxy scan is a textual scan of the non-test source for a client builder, so a client built some other way (a helper that constructs the builder elsewhere, a WASM plugin's egress) is not covered, and it shows the call is present, not that each client is exercised with an ambient proxy set. The wiring of the guarded client is shown on the shared builder, not on each plugin that calls it. The window between vultrino's lookup and the proxy's own lookup is not closed: a name that resolves here can resolve to an internal address at the proxy. The OAuth token-URL check shares the helper but is not shown by this detector.

claims.statement: A url_match pattern on a Deny rule, or on a Prompt rule in a policy whose default_action is not deny, that is an exact URL or path with no wildcard and no query (a request with a query string appended slips past it), or that holds a ? claims.statement: For every policy the write path accepts (refuse_warned_url_patterns), over a grid of 20 url_match patterns (globs with a literal tail, character classes, exact, prefix, host-only, port, query-bearing and path-only), 14 URLs, Deny, Prompt and Allow rules, 5 condition shapes (plain, and with a method, or with a method, not not, not), 3 policy defaults and with or without an Allow rule over the same host, the engine's decision is never weaker than the decision of an engine whose url_match matches exactly what it says (the unbroadened reference in the test), for the URL as sent and with a query parameter appended, and a URL with a query parameter appended (?x=1, or &x=1 when it has a query), with one trailing / added to its path, or with a parameter inserted before its own, is at least as strict as the URL without it (Allow < Prompt < Deny). A Deny or Prompt pattern holding a ? is refused at write. A Deny or Prompt url_match also matches the URL with trailing query parameters removed, with trailing / characters removed and with ;name=value path parameters removed, flipped under each not. A Prompt rule's widened match applies only when the unbroadened decision is Allow, so on the shape govder compiles (a policy with a Deny default holding a Prompt on an exact URL and a method) the exact URL prompts and its query and slash variants stay Denied, for the five money and compliance globs of the shipped packs, absolute and relative; with a second policy that allows everything, those variants are Prompted, never Allowed. A Prompt rule's wide reading does not charge its rate limit: on govder's rate-limited compiled shape (and of action_match, url_match, method and a rate_limit, a Prompt, a Deny default) any number of denied query or slash variants leaves the exact URL's budget intact. The wide reading also reads %2F as / and collapses repeated / in the path, so //v1/refunds, /v1//refunds, /v1%2Frefunds, /;x=1/admin and /x/..%2Fadmin are Denied by a Deny glob written for the plain path. A Prompt under a single not is in the grid.

claims.does_not_establish: Only the listed patterns, URLs and shapes, not every pattern; a property of the engine decision, not a proof. A pattern holding a ? is refused on Deny and Prompt rules, not matched; an Allow rule with a ? is accepted and only narrows. Trailing slashes, ;name=value path parameters, repeated / and %2F are tried; any other rewrite a particular backend applies (case folding of the path, unicode normalisation, backslashes) is not, so a Deny pattern can still be slipped past by those spellings. A server that treats the trailing-slash path as a different resource is over-denied, not under-denied. The Prompt widening can upgrade an Allow to a Prompt, so a request an Allow rule alone would have let through can reach an approver. A Prompt rule's exact reading charges its rate limit once and its wide reading does not charge, so under the wide reading a rate limit counts as within its limit (wider, fail-closed); a widened Prompt match that turns an Allow into a Prompt has already charged the Allow rule's rate limit. Other policies and rule kinds (rate limits, principal or time conditions) are not in the grid. Which deployed vaults hold a policy relying on the old narrower matching is not checked.

claims.statement: The Anthropic workspace on an outgoing request is the operator's, never the caller's, on every path that reaches a plugin: /llm, POST /api/v1/execute, the MCP http_request tool and approval replay. The workspace id is stored on the credential (metadata key anthropic_workspace_id). Before dispatch, any caller-supplied anthropic-workspace-id header (any case) is removed from the request, and the credential's value, if it has one, is written; a credential with none sends none, so the caller cannot choose a workspace with the same bearer on any of these paths. The http plugin repeats the same removal and write on its own parameters. The id must be wrkspc_ plus 8 to 64 ASCII letters or digits: the CLI metadata set command and credential creation refuse anything else, and a stored value that fails the check at use time is refused (the request fails before any upstream call, shown by no meter event, and before the use token is consumed, shown by its use count staying 0) instead of being written into a header. The refusal is a credential configuration error, not an upstream failure: /llm answers 500 with a message naming the misconfigured credential metadata, and an approval-gated request refuses at approval open (no approval is stored) rather than opening an approval that could only fail on resume.
